questions.prompt: What is the main difference between cash-game chips and tournament chips?

choices.text: Cash chips represent real money you can leave with; tournament chips are only tournament equity.
Tournament chips are always worth more dollars than cash chips.
Cash chips expire at the end of each orbit; tournament chips do not.

questions.prompt: In a typical live cash game, when can you leave the table?

choices.text: Only after you win a big pot.
Generally anytime between hands (house rules permitting).
Only when the tournament clock hits a break.
Never until the dealer forces a table change.

Both formats keep identical blind schedules for fairness.
Cash blinds stay at fixed stakes; tournament blinds escalate on a clock.
Live cash has no blinds; only tournaments use blinds.

questions.prompt: If you lose your whole stack in a live cash game, what usually happens next?

choices.text: You are eliminated from the casino for the day.
You may rebuy (or leave); the game continues without a tournament finish.
You automatically win the next hand as compensation.
The dealer converts your empty seat into a tournament bubble.

Because tournaments always start with more chips than cash games.

questions.explanation: Fixed blinds plus optional reloads keep many cash tables deep. Escalating tournament blinds shrink stacks as the event progresses.

choices.text: Blinds are $1 and $2; you may buy in between $100 and $300.
The tournament starts at level 1 and ends at level 2.
You must buy in for exactly $200 every orbit.
The big blind doubles every 20 minutes.

questions.explanation: Cash stakes are fixed blinds plus a buy-in range, not a tournament clock.

choices.text: Heads-up

questions.prompt: Effective stack is best described as…

The smallest stack that can still contest the pot between the players involved.
The sum of every chip on the table.
Only the big blind amount.

choices.text: Deeper stacks remove all postflop decisions.
The button must fold every hand when deep.
Blinds disappear once stacks exceed 100 big blinds.
More streets remain, so acting last gains more information.

choices.text: You are eliminated from the casino event.
Rebuy within the table cap, or rack up and leave.
Wait for the bubble to burst.
The dealer must seat you in a satellite.

A time-charge cash game with constant blinds

240 big blinds
40 big blinds
The big blind only

choices.text: Cash games ban the button.
Cash chips have no dollar value.
You must play until one player has every chip.
You can leave between hands and chips represent withdrawable money.

The dealer position, last to act postflop.
Always the big blind.

Buying in again and again to 'get even tonight'.

Take a walk or end the session.

Sit down in a new game while still dealt into the old one.

questions.explanation: One live hand at a time. Changes go through staff.

questions.prompt: A player wants you to soft-play their friend. The correct response is…

choices.text: Agree if the game is casual.
Check-raise only their friend.
Show them your cards each hand.
Refuse. Soft-playing a partner is collusion.

questions.explanation: Playing a private alliance against the table is cheating, not etiquette.

questions.prompt: The floor's job in a dispute is to…

choices.text: Apply the house rules to the facts.
Award the pot to the regular.
Poll the table and take a vote.
Ignore the dealer.

questions.explanation: The floor decides procedure. It is not a popularity contest.

questions.prompt: Your cards hit the muck by accident and are irretrievably mixed. Expect…

choices.text: A guaranteed refund of the pot.
A dead hand, unless the dealer can still clearly identify them.
An automatic win.
A new deal of only your cards.

questions.explanation: Fouled or indistinguishable cards are usually dead. Protect them before that happens.

questions.prompt: Acting in turn matters because…

choices.text: It lets you see future cards.
The button can skip seats.
Out-of-turn action changes what later players do and may bind you.
Only the big blind may speak.

questions.explanation: Order of action is part of the game, not a courtesy.

questions.prompt: Which request is appropriate?

choices.text: Show me the cards you folded last hand.
Let me use your account to hold my chips.
Tell me what to bet; I will raise you back.
Dealer, please count the pot before I call.

questions.explanation: A pot count is normal. Fishing for folded cards, sharing accounts, or chip-dumping is not.

questions.prompt: $1/$2 with a $200 stack is…

choices.text: 50 big blinds.
100 big blinds.
200 big blinds.
2 big blinds.

questions.explanation: Divide the stack by the big blind. 200 / 2 = 100.

questions.prompt: A pot-sized bet into a $40 pot is…
questions.explanation: Pot-sized means the amount already in the pot, before your bet.

questions.prompt: You are asked to call $25 into a $100 pot. The final pot if you call is…
questions.explanation: The $25 is added to the $100, so you risk 25 to win 125, and the pot becomes 150.

questions.prompt: Converting everything to big blinds helps because…

choices.text: Chips of different colors cannot be counted.
The casino requires BB speech.
Dollars are illegal at the table.
Stakes change, but 100 big blinds means the same depth at $1/$2 or $2/$5.

questions.explanation: Big blinds compare depth across stake sizes.

questions.prompt: $2/$5. Both blinds fold after you open to $15 and the button calls $15. Pot going to the flop is…

choices.text: $32: the $2, the $5, your $15, and the button's $15.
$30, ignoring blinds.

questions.explanation: Posted blinds stay in the pot even when those players fold.

questions.prompt: If you lose the count, the reliable fix is…

choices.text: Guess from chip height.
Ask the dealer to count the pot.
Let the bettor announce a number and ship it.
Add only the last bet.

questions.explanation: A dealer count is a normal request before a big decision.

questions.prompt: Hero shoves $90 into $30 and a covering player calls $90. Pot at showdown is…
A half-pot bet into $60 is…
questions.explanation: Half of 60 is 30.

questions.prompt: $5/$10, stack of $1,000. Depth is…

choices.text: 100 big blinds.
200 big blinds.
50 big blinds.
1,000 big blinds.

questions.explanation: 1000 / 10 = 100 big blinds.

questions.prompt: Call $40 into a pot that will be $160 after your call. You are risking 40 to win…
questions.explanation: The $160 includes your call, so the amount you win if they are bluffing is $120.

questions.prompt: Which count is wrong?

choices.text: A $15 bet into $45 is one-third pot.
A $50 call into a $50 pot makes the final pot $50.
Two $25 calls of a $25 bet add $75 to the previous pot.

questions.explanation: A $50 pot plus a $50 call becomes $100, not $50.

questions.prompt: Before a big call, the disciplined step is…

choices.text: Guess the pot from the chip pile's height.
Trust the bettor's announced pot.
Skip the count because live pots are unknowable.
Confirm the bet size and the pot.

questions.explanation: Price first, then decide. Do not skip the count on a large call.

questions.prompt: A flush draw on the flop has how many outs to the flush, if no pair outs are counted?
questions.explanation: There are 13 cards of the suit and you already see 4, so 9 remain.

questions.prompt: An open-ended straight draw on the flop has…

choices.text: 2 outs.
8 outs.
9 outs.
1 out.

questions.explanation: Four cards on each end complete the straight, so eight outs.

questions.prompt: The rule of 2 and 4 says a 9-out draw has about…

choices.text: 9% on the flop to the river.
2% on the river.
About 36% from the flop to the river, and about 18% with one card to come.
50% exactly.

questions.explanation: Multiply outs by 4 with two cards to come, or by 2 with one. 9×4=36, 9×2=18.

questions.prompt: Equity is not the same as realization because…

choices.text: Outs are always paid in full.
Position and future bets do not matter.
A draw cannot win unimproved.
You may not get to see all the cards, or you may win extra when you hit.

questions.explanation: Fold equity, position, and stacks change how much of your raw equity you keep.

questions.prompt: Turn, 8 clean outs, one card left. A fair quick estimate is…

choices.text: About 16%.

questions.explanation: Eight outs times two is about 16 percent with one card to come.

questions.prompt: Flop, you have a nut flush draw and one overcard. A careful count is…

choices.text: Nine flush outs, plus any overcard outs that are still clean against the betting range.
The nuts already.
Two outs total.
Zero equity if someone bets.

questions.explanation: Do not turn the overcard into extra flush outs. Add it only if that card actually wins.

questions.prompt: You have 4 outs on the river. Calling is mainly about…

choices.text: Always calling because any out can hit.
The suit color.
Whether the price is better than about 8%, and whether the out is clean.
The button's mood.

questions.explanation: Four outs is about 8 percent. You need a very good price, and the out must actually win.

questions.prompt: A gutshot has…

choices.text: 8 outs.
9 outs.
12 outs.
4 outs.

questions.explanation: Only one rank completes a gutshot, and there are four cards of that rank.

questions.prompt: Which draw has more raw outs on the flop?

choices.text: A flush draw (9) versus a gutshot (4).
A gutshot versus a flush draw.
One overcard versus a flush draw.
A backdoor draw versus a made flush.

questions.explanation: Nine flush outs is more than four gutshot outs.

questions.prompt: Rule of 4 is for…

choices.text: The river only.
The flop, with two cards still to come.
Preflop all-ins only.
Counting the pot.

questions.explanation: Two cards to come, multiply outs by about four.

questions.prompt: An out is dirty when…

choices.text: It is the same color as the felt.
It completes your hand and also completes a better hand for the opponent.
It is an ace.
The dealer burns it.

questions.explanation: A dirty out gives you a hand that still loses.

questions.prompt: Seeing both remaining cards is more likely when…

choices.text: You are all-in or the price to continue is small relative to the chance you hit.
You fold.
You bet huge with no fold equity and no draw.
Stacks are deep and you will fold every turn.

questions.explanation: All-in equity is raw equity. As a favorite to fold later, you realize less.

questions.prompt: Pot odds are…

choices.text: The price of a call compared with the pot you can win.
Your probability of winning the tournament.
The rake percentage only.
A required bluff on the river.

questions.explanation: You compare the cost of calling with the size of the pot you are calling into.

questions.prompt: Call $20 into a pot that already has $80 in it, and your call closes the action. You are getting…

choices.text: 1 to 1.
5 to 1, because you win 100 for a 20 call if the $80 includes only the current pot before your call — recount: risk 20 to win 100.
Even money on a $20 pot.

questions.explanation: If $80 is already there and nobody else can raise, you risk 20 to win 100. That is 5 to 1.

questions.prompt: A call is immediately profitable on raw equity when…

choices.text: You feel confident.
The player seems weak.
Your chance of winning is higher than the break-even percent of the price.
You have position, even with zero equity.

questions.explanation: Break-even percent is call / (pot you win + call). Equity above that is a profitable call if the out is clean and there is no more betting.

questions.prompt: Fold equity is…

choices.text: The equity of a folded hand you already mucked.
The chance you hit a flush.
The rake.
The extra value from opponents folding when you bet.

questions.explanation: A bet can win immediately when they fold, which a pure check cannot do.

questions.prompt: You must call $10 into a $40 pot. Break-even equity is about…
questions.explanation: Risk 10 to win 50 total after the call, so 10/50 = 20%. Or 10/(40+10).

questions.prompt: You have about 32% equity with a flush draw on the flop and the pot offers you 4 to 1. If you will see both cards…

choices.text: The price is better than 20% break-even, so a call can be fine before implied odds.
You must fold every draw.
4 to 1 means you need 50%.
Pot odds ignore the number of outs.

questions.explanation: 4 to 1 is 20 percent. Thirty-two percent clears that price if the draw is clean and you see both cards.

questions.prompt: A bluff that risks $50 to win $50 needs to work…

choices.text: More than 75% of the time.
Never; bluffs are free.
More than half the time if you never win when called.
Less than 10% of the time.

questions.explanation: Risk 50 to win 50 is even money. With no showdown value you need folds more than half the time.

questions.prompt: Which statement about EV is right?

choices.text: A winning session proves every call was correct.
Losing a called bluff means the call was a mistake.
You should never call without the nuts.
A +EV call can still lose this particular hand.

questions.explanation: One result is not the decision. EV is the average over the chances.

questions.prompt: Break-even percent for a call of $25 into $75 is…
You have 9% equity and the price requires 25%. A pure call is…

choices.text: Close.
Not justified on pot odds alone.
Mandatory because you have outs.
Profitable because 9 is an odd number.

questions.explanation: Nine percent does not clear a twenty-five percent price.

questions.prompt: Betting can be better than calling when…

choices.text: You have no hand and no fold equity.
The pot is zero.
Fold equity or protection adds value you do not get by only calling.
You are facing an all-in and cannot bet.

questions.explanation: If they can still fold or you deny their equity, betting is a different action from calling.

questions.prompt: Results-oriented thinking sounds like…

choices.text: I called because the price was right, and this time I lost.
I will review the price, not the one outcome.
Variance exists.
I lost, so the call was wrong and I should chase it back.

questions.explanation: Chasing a single loss is not a pot-odds calculation.

questions.prompt: Implied odds are…

choices.text: Chips you expect to win later when you hit, beyond the current pot.
The current pot only.
The rake.
A rule that you may call any bet with a draw.

questions.explanation: They matter when stacks remain and you can get paid on later streets.

questions.prompt: Reverse implied odds are…

choices.text: Extra chips you win with the nuts.
Extra chips you lose when you hit a second-best hand.
The same as pot odds.
A tournament bounty.

questions.explanation: Dominated draws and weak pairs can 'hit' and still lose a big pot.

questions.prompt: Implied odds are weaker when…

choices.text: Stacks are deep and the opponent will pay you off.
You have the nuts when you hit.
You are already all-in, or the opponent will not pay a large bet.
Position lets you control the pot.

questions.explanation: If there is no more money to win, only the current price matters.

questions.prompt: A small pair calling a huge raise out of position, deep, mainly risks…

choices.text: Too many immediate pot odds, which are excellent.
Missing the rule of 4.
Being unable to bluff the river with air only.
Reverse implied odds: you flop a set rarely, and you often face large bets when you miss or are dominated.

questions.explanation: Set-mining needs the right price and the right stacks. It is not an automatic call.

questions.prompt: You are all-in on the flop with a draw. Which odds matter?

choices.text: Pot odds and raw equity. There are no future bets to imply.
Only implied odds.
Only reverse implied odds from later bets.
Neither, because all-in pots are not real.

questions.explanation: Once all-in, the rest of the cards are free. Use equity versus the current pot.

questions.prompt: Deep stacks and a nut flush draw in position improve…

choices.text: Nothing.
Implied odds, because you can still win more when you hit.
The number of flush outs from 9 to 15.
The board texture by itself.

questions.explanation: Position and leftover stacks let you extract more on later streets.

questions.prompt: Calling a large river bet with a bluff-catcher is not an implied-odds call because…

choices.text: The river still has two cards to come.
You can still bet later.
There is no later street. You are deciding on the current price.
Pot odds expire on the river.

questions.explanation: Implied odds need future betting. The river is the last card.

questions.prompt: A dominated flush draw (you have the low flush draw, they can have the nut draw) has…

choices.text: Perfect implied odds.
Nine outs that always win.
No reverse implied odds.
Reverse implied odds: some of your flush cards still lose.

questions.explanation: Do not count outs that make you second best as clean.

questions.prompt: Best spot for implied odds?

choices.text: Deep stacks, nutted draw, opponent likely to pay.
All-in for a few chips with air.
River call with ace-high.
A short stack already committed.

questions.explanation: You need money behind and a hand that can get paid when it hits.

questions.prompt: Worst misuse of implied odds?

choices.text: Folding a draw that is not getting the right price and will not get paid.
Calling too much because 'I might hit and stack them' with no plan.
Counting nine clean flush outs.
Using pot odds when stacks are all-in.

questions.explanation: Implied odds are not a reason to ignore a terrible price.

questions.prompt: Rake and a tip reduce…

choices.text: The number of outs.
Your position.
The net pot you actually win.
The big blind.

questions.explanation: What you keep is smaller than the chips in the middle. Tight games feel this more.

questions.prompt: Set-mining a pair is more reasonable when…

choices.text: The raise is huge and stacks are shallow.
You are out of position against a nit who will not pay a set.
You will stack off without a set.
The call is small relative to the effective stack you can win when you flop a set.

questions.explanation: A common live guide is a small price versus a deep stack, not a huge call versus a short stack.

questions.prompt: A poker range is…

choices.text: The set of hands a player can still have, not one exact hand.
The single hand you put them on.
Only the nuts.
The board.

questions.explanation: Live reads start with every hand that would take the line, then remove what the line folds.

questions.prompt: How many combinations of ace-king are in a fresh deck?
questions.explanation: AK offsuit has 12 combinations and AK suited has 4, totaling 16.

questions.prompt: How many pocket-pair combinations of pocket aces?
questions.explanation: Choose 2 suits of the ace from 4: 4×3/2 = 6.

questions.prompt: Why remove combinations as the hand continues?

choices.text: To make the range always 50%.
Because folded cards stay in the range.
Because the board does not matter.
Betting, calling, and board cards make some holdings impossible or unlikely.

questions.explanation: A tight player's check-raise removes many weak hands they would not play that way.

questions.prompt: Board is Ah 7c 2d. How many ace-king combinations remain?

choices.text: 12. One ace is on the board, so the 4 suited AK with that ace are impossible and 12 offsuit-or-other-suit combinations remain from the original 16.

questions.explanation: Four aces existed. One is visible, so each AK combo using that ace is gone. 16 − 4 = 12.

questions.prompt: Pocket pairs are fewer than offsuit broadways because…

choices.text: Pairs use two cards of the same rank, and there are only six suit pairings.
Pairs are illegal.
Offsuit hands have six combinations.
The deck has more ranks than suits.

questions.explanation: Each pocket pair has six combinations. A specific offsuit hand like AKo has twelve.

questions.prompt: If a nit 3-bets and you block aces with an ace in your hand…

choices.text: They have more ace combinations.
Blockers do nothing.
You reduce the combinations of strong aces they can hold.
You guarantee they are bluffing.

questions.explanation: A blocker removes some strong combos. It does not prove a bluff.

questions.prompt: Putting someone on exactly 7h 2c after one limp is…

choices.text: Sound range construction.
Required before every call.
Better than listing a range.
Too narrow. Start with the hands that take the action.

questions.explanation: One exact hand is a guess. A range can be updated.

questions.prompt: Which count is correct?

choices.text: Pocket kings: 16 combinations.
Pocket kings: 6 combinations.
AK suited: 12 combinations.
One specific suited hand: 6 combinations.

questions.explanation: Any pocket pair has 6 combos. One specific suited hand has 4. AKo has 12.

questions.prompt: A range gets tighter when…

choices.text: The player, the position, and the line remove weak hands.
You want them to be bluffing.
The pot is small.
You have not watched them.

questions.explanation: Tight lines and tight players delete combinations. Hope does not.

questions.prompt: Using ranges at the table should stay…

choices.text: A full solver printout mid-hand.
An excuse to ignore the action.
A short list you can actually use: value, draws, and bluffs that took this line.
Secret, so you never check it against the board.

questions.explanation: A usable range is small enough to count and still honest about the line.

questions.prompt: Blockers are most useful when…

choices.text: You ignore the opponent's range.
Every river call is a bluff-catch.
You hold a card they need for their value hands or their bluffs.
You want a reason to call without pot odds.

questions.explanation: A blocker changes the mix. It does not replace the price or the line.
